tool.name: LoCoHStandard
tool.summary: Standard (fixed-k) Local Convex Hull (LoCoH) home-range and utilization-distribution estimator (Getz and Wilmers 2004).
tool.usage:
Choosing k: small k produces tighter, more fragmented hulls that capture fine structure and hard boundaries (rivers, cliffs, habitat edges), while large k produces smoother, more contiguous ranges; k equal to the number of points reduces to the minimum convex polygon. k must be at least 3 and no greater than the number of points.
Getz and Wilmers (2004) recommend the "minimum spurious hole covering" (MSHC) rule: select the smallest k that fills spurious holes so the covering attains the correct topology; plotting isopleth area (or the number of holes) against k helps locate where the area levels off. As a heuristic starting value, Getz et al. (2007) suggest k equal to the square root of the number of points (k1 = sqrt(n)), then refining toward the value that minimizes the combined Type I and Type II error.
The T-LoCoH R package (Lyons, Turner and Getz 2013) recommends selecting the parameter empirically rather than by a fixed formula: build hull sets over a range of k values and inspect how isopleth area and spurious holes change, choosing the value just before isopleth areas begin to over-inflate.
Screen out obvious location errors before running, as LoCoH is sensitive to outliers.
References: Getz and Wilmers (2004) Ecography 27:489-505, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0906-7590.2004.03835.x Getz et al. (2007) PLoS ONE 2(2):e207, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0000207 Lyons, Turner and Getz (2013) Movement Ecology 1:2, https://doi.org/10.1186/2051-3933-1-2
Environments: this tool honors the Output Coordinate System environment. If it is set to a coordinate system other than the input's, the output polygons are reprojected to it as a last step; areas, point counts, and densities remain computed in the input coordinate system. No other geoprocessing environments affect this tool.

dialogReference.para: The point features (for example, GPS or VHF telemetry fixes) from which the local hulls are built. May be in a geographic or projected coordinate system; empty or null geometries are ignored.

The number of nearest neighbors used to build each local convex hull, including the focal point itself, so each hull is formed from a point and its k-1 nearest neighbors. Must be at least 3 and no greater than the number of input points.

Output polygon feature class of the dissolved cumulative LoCoH isopleths. Each feature stores its dissolved area (Area), the number of input points it encloses (Point_Count), and the proportion of all points enclosed (Point_Proportion).
Optional output polygon feature class of the individual local convex hulls. Each hull stores its own area and the cumulative point count and proportion at its position in the area-sorted sequence.

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Standard (fixed-k) Local Convex Hull (LoCoH) home-range and utilization-distribution estimator (Getz and Wilmers 2004).
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Estimates an animal's home range and utilization distribution using the Standard (fixed-k) Local Convex Hull (LoCoH) method of Getz and Wilmers (2004). For every input point, the tool builds the convex hull of that point plus its k-1 nearest neighbors (k points total). Hulls are sorted by area from smallest to largest and merged cumulatively; each cumulative union is a density isopleth, and the proportion of all points it encloses defines its utilization level (for example, the 95% isopleth approximates the home-range boundary while excluding outlying excursions). The primary output is a polygon feature class of the dissolved cumulative isopleths, each attributed with its area, the number of enclosed points, and the point proportion; an optional second output contains the individual local hulls. Distances and areas honor the input coordinate system: Haversine distance and WGS84 spheroidal area for geographic data, planar distance and area for projected data. LoCoH is well suited to ranges with hard boundaries such as rivers, cliffs, or habitat edges that kernel methods tend to smooth over. Method reference: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0906-7590.2004.03835.x
